analysis.one_liner: Bans car insurers from pricing policies using credit scores, occupation, education, gender, and similar factors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote; five House Democrats backed it and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred private passenger auto insurers from setting rates or deciding eligibility based on gender, education, occupation, employment status, homeownership, ZIP code, census tract, marital status, credit score, consumer reports, or previous insurance history. It would also have required insurers to prove to the FTC every two years that their marketing, underwriting, rating, claims handling, and fraud investigations do not disadvantage customers by race, sex, disability, or similar traits, and to make their underwriting rules and rate filings public. The FTC could treat violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and consumers and states could sue.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers with low incomes, poor credit, less education, or no home — people who today can be charged more for the same coverage despite a clean driving record, or steered into a pricier affiliate company's policy. All car insurance customers would also gain access to the underwriting rules and rate filings now treated as trade secrets.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insurers and their affiliates from considering gender, education, occupation, employment status, homeownership, ZIP code, census tract, marital status, credit score, consumer reports, previous insurer, or prior purchase history in setting rates or eligibility [S3].

Requires every auto insurer to submit information to the FTC every two years showing its marketing, underwriting, rating, claims handling, fraud investigations, and algorithms do not disparately impact customers by race, national origin, religion, sex, sexual orientation, disability, or gender identity [S3].
Makes all underwriting rules and rate filings available for public inspection and bars insurers from treating them as proprietary trade secrets [S3].

Gives consumers the right to sue for damages, punitive damages for willful violations, and attorney's fees, and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents; the FTC can enforce violations as unfair or deceptive practices with a civil penalty of at least $2,500 per violation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Auto insurers, whose pricing models and profitability from income-proxy rating variables (the bill's findings say these push higher rates onto lower-income drivers [S3]) would have to change. Some drivers who currently benefit from those variables — homeowners, married drivers, drivers with strong credit — could see their discounts shrink, and credit reporting companies would lose a stream of data sales to insurers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Auto insurers and credit data sellers

drawbacks.text: Insurers use credit scores and similar variables because they correlate with claims losses; the bill's own findings acknowledge the variables relate to profitability, so removing them could push rates up for some drivers whose profiles insurers currently price as lower-risk [S3].

The bill moves pricing oversight toward the FTC, an agency that historically has not regulated insurance, on top of existing state insurance regulators, raising questions about which regulator is responsible and how complex the new compliance burden would be [S2].

The rule of construction makes a violation occur whenever a prohibited factor prevents a consumer from getting the lowest rate available to that consumer, a standard that could be hard for insurers to satisfy or for courts to apply consistently [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For drivers with poor credit, low income, or no home, the benefit is direct and large: their driving record, not their income proxies, would set their rate. The honest cost is that some drivers who now get preferred rates through those variables would pay more, since insurers would need to rebuild their pricing on driving-related factors. Making rate filings public would also expose pricing that has been effectively secret. The bill was a broad rewrite of how a state-regulated industry sets prices, so implementation would have been contentious.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services and Energy and Commerce committees, then to a Financial Services subcommittee, and never got a markup or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the bill on June 6, 2023, joined by Representatives Rashida Tlaib and Mark Takano as original sponsors [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services and in addition to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced [S5].
Three days later it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, which is the last recorded action; no markup, hearing, or floor vote is listed [S5].
Four House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor is listed [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died with it and would need to be reintroduced to move again [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Auto insurers keep their existing pricing models, including credit scores and other income proxies, and face no new FTC reporting or public-disclosure requirements. Credit reporting companies keep selling data to insurers.

for.name: Reps. Rashida Tlaib and Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill

against.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup; the bill sat on the Innovation, Data, and Commerce subcommittee referral for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill after its dual referral to Energy and Commerce

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill — five House Democrats in total, with no Republican support listed — but no vote ever occurred, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have banned the income-proxy variables insurers use to charge higher rates to lower-income drivers and required public disclosure of underwriting rules and rate filings now treated as trade secrets. Insurers' ability to price by those variables is exactly what the bill targeted [S3].

industries.industry: Credit reporting agencies and consumer data sellers
industries.note: Insurers could no longer use credit scores, credit-based insurance scores, or consumer reports, removing a major data sale and the pricing advantage built on it [S3].
